chunks.title: Zero-trust networking principles applied to cloud workloads
chunks.content:
Zero-trust networking principles applied to cloud workloads

Zero trust replaces the perimeter model ('inside the VPC = trusted') with the assumption that the network is hostile. Every request is authenticated, authorized, and encrypted regardless of source. In cloud, this manifests as: (1) identity-based access control (SG referencing SG, IAM, mTLS) instead of IP allowlists, (2) default-deny everywhere, (3) encryption in transit between every component including same-VPC traffic, (4) short-lived credentials for both humans and workloads.

Decision rules:
- DEFAULT-DENY at every boundary: SG default outbound is permissive — explicitly restrict it
- PREFER identity over IP: SG-to-SG references, IAM auth on RDS, mTLS in service mesh
- ENCRYPT in transit always — TLS even for in-VPC traffic; ALB→target should use TLS not HTTP
- ELIMINATE flat networks — segment by tier (web/app/data) and by trust domain (prod/non-prod/shared)
- AUTHENTICATE every service-to-service call (SPIFFE/mTLS or signed JWT), do not rely on network position

Trade-offs:
- Strict default-deny: secure but causes outages during deploys until policies catch up — pair with staging that mirrors prod policies
- mTLS everywhere: strong identity but cert lifecycle complexity — service mesh (Istio/Linkerd) amortizes the cost
- Identity-based controls: scales with services not IPs but requires the identity plane (IAM, SPIFFE) to be highly available

Anti-patterns:
- 0.0.0.0/0 in security group ingress on application ports
- Flat /16 VPC with no tier separation — one compromised pod reaches the database
- Treating private IP space as 'trusted' — RFC1918 is not a security boundary
- Plaintext HTTP between microservices because 'it's internal'

chunks.title: When to use Security Groups, when to use Network ACLs
chunks.content:
When to use Security Groups, when to use Network ACLs

Security Groups are stateful, instance-level, allow-only firewalls referenced by ID. NACLs are stateless, subnet-level, allow+deny firewalls. They are not interchangeable: SGs are the primary control plane and should carry 95% of the policy. NACLs are a coarse second layer for blast-radius control (e.g. block a known-bad CIDR across an entire subnet) and for explicit denies that SGs cannot express.

Decision rules:
- USE Security Groups as the primary firewall — write rules referencing other SG IDs, not IPs, where possible
- USE NACLs only for: (a) wholesale CIDR blocks, (b) compliance requirements for explicit deny, (c) defense-in-depth at subnet edge
- KEEP NACLs simple — stateless rules force you to allow ephemeral return ports (1024-65535) which is error-prone
- PREFER one SG per role (web-sg, app-sg, db-sg) referencing each other, over per-instance custom SGs
- AUDIT SGs for 0.0.0.0/0 ingress on non-public ports — common via Access Analyzer or `aws ec2 describe-security-groups`

Trade-offs:
- SG-to-SG references: identity-based and clean but limited to 60 rules per SG (soft limit)
- NACL deny lists: powerful but stateless rules require careful return-port handling
- Multiple SGs per ENI (up to 5): flexible composition vs harder to reason about effective policy

Anti-patterns:
- Replicating SG rules in NACLs — doubles maintenance, no security benefit
- Allowing 0.0.0.0/0 on port 22 (SSH) — use Systems Manager Session Manager instead, no inbound port required
- Using NACLs to control individual application ports — SGs are the right layer
- One giant SG attached to everything — defeats segmentation

chunks.title: Eliminating internet egress for AWS service traffic
chunks.content:
Eliminating internet egress for AWS service traffic

By default, an EC2 instance in a private subnet calling S3 routes through a NAT gateway and the public internet. VPC Endpoints (Gateway endpoints for S3/DynamoDB; Interface endpoints / PrivateLink for everything else) route this traffic over the AWS backbone, never traversing the internet. This eliminates NAT data-processing cost, reduces attack surface, and enables endpoint policies for fine-grained control.

Decision rules:
- USE Gateway endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB — free, applied via route table, no per-hour cost
- USE Interface endpoints (PrivateLink) for: SSM, Secrets Manager, KMS, ECR, STS, CloudWatch Logs, SQS
- ATTACH endpoint policies that scope which buckets/keys can be reached from the VPC — defense against data exfil
- BLOCK NAT egress for AWS API calls once endpoints are deployed — forces traffic through audited path
- USE PrivateLink to expose your own services across accounts/VPCs without VPC peering or public exposure

Trade-offs:
- Interface endpoints: ~$0.01/hour/AZ + data — adds up across many endpoints, but typically cheaper than NAT for high-volume API traffic
- Endpoint policies: extra control plane vs another place to misconfigure
- Gateway endpoints: free but only S3/DynamoDB

Anti-patterns:
- Routing all AWS API traffic through NAT — expensive and exposes the call to internet path
- Endpoint policy of `*` — defeats the purpose; scope to required buckets/regions
- VPC peering when PrivateLink would do — peering creates a transitive trust risk

metadata.title: Eliminating internet egress for AWS service traffic

chunks.title: Transit Gateway vs VPC Peering vs PrivateLink
chunks.content:
Transit Gateway vs VPC Peering vs PrivateLink

At small scale (2-3 VPCs), VPC peering is cheapest. Beyond that, Transit Gateway becomes the right primitive: it is a hub-and-spoke router that supports route tables per attachment, scales to thousands of VPCs, and integrates with on-premises (Direct Connect, VPN). PrivateLink is orthogonal — it exposes a single service without making the whole VPC reachable, which is the right answer for SaaS-like inter-team service exposure.

Decision rules:
- USE VPC Peering only for ≤3 VPCs with stable, predictable mesh topology
- USE Transit Gateway when you have 3+ VPCs, multi-account, or hybrid (on-prem) connectivity
- USE PrivateLink for service-level exposure — when the consumer needs ONE service, not a whole VPC
- SEGMENT TGW with route tables — prod, non-prod, shared-services should be separate route tables on the same TGW
- AVOID transitive routing across peering — peering is non-transitive by design; TGW is the right answer

Trade-offs:
- TGW: scalable but ~$0.05/hour/attachment + data — costlier than peering at small scale
- Peering: cheap but explodes to N*(N-1)/2 connections — unmanageable past ~5 VPCs
- PrivateLink: tightest exposure but per-service setup; not suitable for general 'two VPCs need to talk'

Anti-patterns:
- Full mesh peering across 10+ VPCs — operational nightmare
- TGW with one shared route table — defeats segmentation, prod sees non-prod
- Routing prod traffic through a non-prod TGW attachment for 'convenience'

chunks.title: Default-deny NetworkPolicy with namespace-scoped egress
chunks.content:
Default-deny NetworkPolicy with namespace-scoped egress

By default, every pod in a Kubernetes cluster can talk to every other pod. This is the largest in-cluster blast-radius problem and the first thing to fix. NetworkPolicy resources implement default-deny + explicit allow at L3/L4. They require a CNI that enforces policy (Calico, Cilium, AWS VPC CNI with policy mode). Production clusters should ship with a default-deny baseline in every namespace and per-app egress rules.

Decision rules:
- APPLY a default-deny ingress + egress NetworkPolicy in every namespace as the baseline
- ALLOW DNS egress (UDP/TCP 53 to kube-system) explicitly — without it, all pod traffic breaks
- SCOPE allow rules using podSelector + namespaceSelector — never allow by IP/CIDR inside the cluster
- ALLOW egress to specific external CIDRs (e.g. database VPC, payment provider) only where required
- TEST policies in a staging cluster identical to prod — NetworkPolicy bugs cause silent partial outages

Trade-offs:
- Default-deny: strong isolation but causes deploy-time breakage if policies lag — gate via CI policy linting
- Calico/Cilium: full L3-L7 policy but adds a CNI dependency vs simpler kube-proxy + AWS VPC CNI
- Cilium with eBPF: highest performance and L7 policy but operational complexity

Anti-patterns:
- Running production without any NetworkPolicy — one compromised pod reaches everything
- Allow-all egress to 0.0.0.0/0 — defeats the purpose, common exfil path
- Forgetting to allow DNS egress — entire namespace silently breaks
- Using AWS VPC CNI without the network policy add-on enabled — NetworkPolicy resources are silently ignored

chunks.title: Service mesh for zero-trust east-west traffic (Istio, Linkerd)
chunks.content:
Service mesh for zero-trust east-west traffic (Istio, Linkerd)

A service mesh terminates and enforces mTLS between every service in the cluster, replacing IP-based trust with cryptographic workload identity (SPIFFE). It also provides L7 authorization policies (e.g. 'service-A can call /v1/charge on service-B'), traffic shifting (canary), and observability. Mesh is the right answer when you have many services, multi-team ownership, or compliance requirements for in-transit encryption.

Decision rules:
- ADOPT a mesh (Linkerd preferred for simplicity, Istio for advanced traffic management) when service count exceeds ~10 or compliance requires in-cluster mTLS
- ENABLE STRICT mTLS mode mesh-wide once all workloads are onboarded — PERMISSIVE is the migration step, not the destination
- WRITE AuthorizationPolicy resources in addition to NetworkPolicy — NetworkPolicy is L3/L4, AuthZ is L7
- CO-DEPLOY mesh with NetworkPolicy — they are layered controls, not alternatives
- MONITOR mesh control-plane health — a failed control plane can break workload-to-workload traffic

Trade-offs:
- Linkerd: simple, fast, Rust data plane vs fewer features than Istio
- Istio: feature-rich (VirtualService, fault injection, ext-authz) vs complexity and resource cost
- Sidecar mode: per-pod overhead vs ambient mode (newer, less mature) reduces footprint

Anti-patterns:
- Adopting Istio for a 5-service cluster — operational complexity exceeds benefit
- Running mesh in PERMISSIVE mode forever — provides no security guarantee
- Skipping NetworkPolicy because 'we have a service mesh' — mesh data plane can be bypassed if pod can talk directly

metadata.title: Service mesh for zero-trust east-west traffic (Istio, Linkerd)
